issues.title: BUG: Out of Bounds Reads with offset/strided views on compiled kernels
issues.author: KyleMylonakisProtopia
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Sections marked as AI analysis are reviewed and edited by me for clarity.

AI Analysis:
> When a tensor that is a view with a non-zero `storage_offset` is passed as a mutated pointer argument to a raw `triton.jit` kernel, `torch.compile` silently produces an incorrect result. This is due to data being read from beyond the end of a buffer into memory.

My Analysis:
At a high level, strided/offset views of tensors can read out of bounds when used with torch compile in some edge cases.

AI Analysis:
> The over-read is normally invisible because the kernel overwrites the whole region. The edge case is when the kernel skips writing part of its output as a performance optimization. E.G "if this row is masked/ignored, return early".

My Analysis:
The primary edge case is when we are dealing with masked tensors, where not all of the tensor is used as a performance optimization.

AI Analysis:
> This bug was originally found when compiling Liger-Kernel's `LigerFusedLinearJSD`  and `LigerFusedLinearCrossEntropy` functions, where it silently corrupted outputs returning incorrect losses compared to eager execution whenever any label was `ignore_index` was present. Both of these failures can be silent.
I introduced a workaround with Liger at https://github.com/linkedin/Liger-Kernel/pull/1338, however the bug is fundamentally in PyTorch.

My Analysis:
I was using those kernels and ran into this bug. You can make a workaround in Liger, but this is a Pytorch bug.

## Reproduction


With AI assistance, I created a script which depends only on `torch` and `triton`.

AI Analysis:
> The script poisons the caching allocator so the
corruption is identifiable. The usual `compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck` does not flag this, because CUDA mappings are page-granular and a small over-read still lands in mapped memory.

My Analysis:
In other words, when the overruns are small enough, you land in your paged memory pool, which is still technically owned by the process and doesn't immediately fault.

The AI reproduction script is

```python
import torch, triton, triton.language as tl

N, R, SKIP, POISON, DEV = 2048, 4, 1, 12345.0, "cuda"

@triton.jit
def maybe_fill(out_ptr, do_write, n_cols, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    """Fill out_ptr[0:n_cols] with 1.0, but only when do_write != 0."""
    if do_write != 0:
        offs = tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
        tl.store(out_ptr + offs, 1.0, mask=offs < n_cols)

def run():
    base = torch.zeros(R, N, device=DEV, dtype=torch.float32)
    for i in range(R):
        row = base[i : i + 1]                       # view, storage_offset = i * N
        maybe_fill[(1,)](row, 0 if i == SKIP else 1, N, BLOCK=N)
        base[i : i + 1] = row                       # write-back
    return base

def poison_allocator(count=2048):
    junk = [torch.full((N,), POISON, device=DEV, dtype=torch.float32) for _ in range(count)]
    del junk
    torch.cuda.synchronize()

expected = torch.zeros(R, N, device=DEV)
expected[[i for i in range(R) if i != SKIP]] = 1.0

poison_allocator(); eager = run().clone()
cf = torch.compile(run, fullgraph=True); cf()      # compile before poisoning
poison_allocator(); compiled = cf().clone()

print("eager    matches:", torch.equal(eager, expected))
print("compiled matches:", torch.equal(compiled, expected))
print("freed-memory value present:", int((compiled == POISON).sum()), "elements")
```

AI Analysis:
> Row `SKIP` is never written by the kernel, so it must remain zero in both runs.

**Observed:**

```text
eager    matches: True
compiled matches: False
freed-memory value present: 2048 elements
```

> The poison value `12345.0` never exists in live tensors. It is written into memory that was freed before the call. Its presence is direct evidence of an out-of-bounds read.

My Analysis:
The AI generated script perfectly captures the bug that we are trying to resolve.

### Mechanism

AI Analysis
> Three different pieces interact to cause the bug. The first two are individually reasonable. The third breaks an
assumption the second one depends on.

> 1. Functionalizing a mutated Triton pointer arg clones it via
   `torch._prims_common.clone_preserve_strides`.

> 2. To preserve the view's layout, that helper has to clone `storage_offset + span` elements out of the tensor's storage, not just the tensor's own elements:

   ```python
   needed_size = compute_required_storage_length(x.size(), x.stride(), x.storage_offset())
   buffer = torch.as_strided(x, (needed_size,), (1,), 0).clone()
   return torch.as_strided(buffer, x.size(), x.stride(), x.storage_offset())
   ```

>  For `base[1:2]` of a `(4, 2048)` tensor that is `2048 + 2048 = 4096` elements. This is correct in eager, where the base storage genuinely has 8192 elements to read from.

> 3. Inductor's `as_strided` lowering has two paths. Which one it takes depends on whether the incoming tensor is still a view:

>   - `x` is an unrealized view over a larger buffer, the lowering unwraps to that buffer, so the offset is resolved against storage that really exists. This is the case the code was written for, and it is fine.
>   - `x` has already been materialized into its own buffer: the lowering takes that buffer as the storage. Inductor materializes a view when it is the output of a fused computation, which is exactly what the `slice_scatter` chain from the write-back produces.

> In the second case the storage is the small buffer of say 2048 elements, and the lowering builds a `ReinterpretView` describing 4096 elements. Nothing checks that the requested `ReinterpretView` extent fits.

My Analysis:
The key failure is in point 3 above. Because the tensor has already been materialized into a buffer of smaller size, when inductor then reinterprets the tensor, it uses the larger size which goes beyond the capacity of the allocated buffer being used for the smaller view. The rest is the particulars of the windowdressing that allows that failure to occur.

AI Analysis:
> So the invariant that breaks is this: `aten.as_strided`'s `storage_offset` is relative to the whole storage, but Inductor resolves it against whichever buffer happened to get realized. Those are the same thing right up until a view gets materialized into a buffer sized to the view, and then the lowering is describing memory that was never allocated.

My Analysis:
The storage_offset is relative to whole whole storage, reading out of bounds to the buffer used by the view.


### What hides this bug

AI Analysis:

> - `do_write` must be a runtime arg, not `tl.constexpr`. As a constexpr, Triton compiles the store away, the pointer is no longer seen as mutated, so no clone is emitted.
> - The mutated arg must be a view whose required extent exceeds its own numel. A non-zero `storage_offset` or gaps between elements must be present.
> - Some runtime path must skip writing, or the garbage is always overwritten.
> - The bug is is shape-dependent. It reproduces at `N = 2048` but not at `N = 1 << 20` because Inductor makes different realization choices.
> - The view must be realized as its own buffer. A single kernel launch on `base[1:2]` with no surrounding computation does not reproduce the bug. The loop with write-backs creates the `slice_scatter` chain that forces per-view realization.

My Analysis:
This bug only shows up when a confluence of factors occur. This is because some of the cases are already correctly handled by Inductor, the bug only materializes when the garbage memory is used in some way, and when inductor actually picks the specific kernels which are broken at compile time.

issues.title: [torch.compile] Inductor-generated Triton module cannot resolve NamedTuple constexpr arguments
issues.author: drisspg
issues.body:
### Human

Ran into this and was surprised that this is not caused a graph break 


This arose while simplifying stride arguments in a custom Triton attention kernel that must continue to work with `torch.compile(fullgraph=True)`.

> **AI assistance disclosure:** The structured report and reproducer below were prepared and executed by an AI assistant at the reporter's request. The reporter reviewed the minimal reproducer and explicitly requested that an issue be filed.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

A Python `NamedTuple` can be passed as a `tl.constexpr` argument to a directly launched Triton kernel, and its fields can be accessed by name inside the kernel. However, compiling the same wrapper with `torch.compile(fullgraph=True)` fails because Inductor serializes the value into generated Python as a `MatrixStrides(...)` expression without defining or importing `MatrixStrides`.

#### Minimal reproducer

```python
from typing import NamedTuple

import torch
import triton
import triton.language as tl


class MatrixStrides(NamedTuple):
    batch: int
    token: int


@triton.jit
def copy_first_row_kernel(
    x_ptr,
    out_ptr,
    N: tl.constexpr,
    X_STRIDES: tl.constexpr,
    BLOCK: tl.constexpr,
):
    offsets = tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
    values = tl.load(
        x_ptr + 0 * X_STRIDES.batch + offsets * X_STRIDES.token,
        mask=offsets < N,
    )
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, values, mask=offsets < N)


def copy_first_row(x):
    out = torch.empty_like(x[0])
    copy_first_row_kernel[(1,)](
        x,
        out,
        N=x.shape[1],
        X_STRIDES=MatrixStrides(
            batch=x.stride(0),
            token=x.stride(1),
        ),
        BLOCK=16,
    )
    return out


x = torch.arange(16, device="cuda").reshape(2, 8)
expected = x[0].clone()

# Direct Triton launch succeeds.
eager = copy_first_row(x)
torch.testing.assert_close(eager, expected)
print("direct Triton launch: PASS")

# Inductor fails while loading generated code.
compiled = torch.compile(copy_first_row, fullgraph=True)
compiled_result = compiled(x)
torch.testing.assert_close(compiled_result, expected)
```

### Expected behavior

Either:

1. Inductor preserves/reconstructs the `NamedTuple` constexpr so the compiled function behaves like the direct Triton launch, or
2. `torch.compile` reports a targeted unsupported-input error instead of emitting generated Python that fails with an unresolved name.

A plain tuple used as `X_STRIDES[0]`/`X_STRIDES[1]` works in both the direct launch and the Inductor path, but loses the named field access supported by Triton itself.

### Error logs

The direct launch prints:

```text
direct Triton launch: PASS
```

The compiled call fails with:

```text
torch._inductor.exc.InductorError: NameError: name 'MatrixStrides' is not defined
```

The relevant generated metadata contains the unresolved constructor:

```python
triton_meta={
    'signature': {
        'x_ptr': '*i64',
        'out_ptr': '*i64',
        'N': 'constexpr',
        'X_STRIDES': 'constexpr',
        'BLOCK': 'constexpr',
    },
    'constants': {
        'N': 8,
        'X_STRIDES': MatrixStrides(batch=8, token=1),
        'BLOCK': 16,
    },
    # ...
}
```

issues.title: [nested compile region] silently incorrect result on global mutation
issues.author: zou3519
issues.body:
```
from dataclasses import dataclass

import torch


@dataclass
class RegionInput:
    hidden: torch.Tensor


region_input = RegionInput(torch.tensor(0))


@torch.compiler.nested_compile_region
def region():
    return region_input.hidden + 1


def fn(hidden):
    global region_input
    for _ in range(2):
        region_input = RegionInput(hidden)
        hidden = region()
    return hidden


hidden = torch.tensor(0)
expected = fn(hidden)
actual = torch.compile(fn, backend="eager", fullgraph=True)(hidden)

print(f"expected: {expected}")
print(f"actual:   {actual}")
```

issues.title: [Inductor] Prefer CUDA Toolkit libdevice for Triton-backed Inductor kernels
issues.author: liqiangxl
issues.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

# Proposal: [Inductor] Prefer CUDA Toolkit libdevice for Triton-backed Inductor kernels

Prepared with the help of codex gpt-5.5

## Summary

Update PyTorch Inductor's Triton libdevice selection so that, by default, it uses the CUDA toolkit's `libdevice.10.bc` when it is available and falls back to Triton's bundled `libdevice.10.bc` when it is not.

This preserves the current explicit override behavior through `TRITON_LIBDEVICE_PATH`, while improving the default path on systems where a compatible CUDA toolkit is installed.

## Motivation

The main motivation is to use the most current compatible CUDA `libdevice.10.bc` available on the system. Triton bundles its own copy of `libdevice.10.bc`, but that **bundled copy can lag the installed CUDA toolkit**. When it lags, Inductor-generated Triton kernels may **miss fixes, numerical updates, or target-specific codegen improvements that are already present in the CUDA toolkit libdevice**.

Recent benchmarking exposed one concrete example: **BF16 GELU kernels using regular `libdevice.tanh` were much faster when Triton linked the CUDA toolkit libdevice instead of Triton's bundled copy**. The bundled libdevice emitted a branchy `__nv_tanhf` implementation, while the installed CUDA toolkit libdevice emitted a branchless form (introduced since cuda-12.8). Setting `TRITON_LIBDEVICE_PATH=/usr/local/cuda-0.gpgpu/nvvm/libdevice/libdevice.10.bc` significantly improved the generated PTX and kernel runtime.

This should not require every PyTorch user to install a full CUDA toolkit. The CUDA toolkit libdevice should be preferred when discoverable, and Triton's bundled libdevice should remain the fallback when it is not.

Today, PyTorch already contains plumbing for selecting the CUDA toolkit libdevice through `torch._inductor.config.eager_numerics.use_pytorch_libdevice` or `config.emulate_precision_casts`. That path is opt-in and for bit-wise accuracy. The proposed change makes toolkit libdevice the preferred default when discoverable.

## Benchmark Check

A targeted torch.compile/Inductor check was run for GELU forward on NVIDIA GB200 with:

- workload: `F.gelu(x + bias, approximate="tanh")`;
- shape: BF16 `[16384, 16384]` input with BF16 `[16384]` bias;
- inputs: `torch.manual_seed(0)`, `x = torch.randn((16384, 16384), device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)`, `bias = torch.randn((16384,), device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16)`;
- compile mode: `torch.compile(dynamic=False, mode="max-autotune-no-cudagraphs")`;
Results:

| libdevice source | median us | mean us | min us |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| CUDA toolkit `/usr/local/cuda/nvvm/libdevice/libdevice.10.bc` | 271.28 | 272.09 | 264.64 |
| Triton bundled `/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/triton/backends/nvidia/lib/libdevice.10.bc` | 329.62 | 331.14 | 319.42 |

The CUDA toolkit libdevice was `1.22x` faster by median for this one-shape check. A short repeat produced similar medians: `270.42 us` for toolkit libdevice and `335.17 us` for Triton's bundled libdevice, or `1.24x` faster with toolkit libdevice.


## Proposed Behavior

Define two concepts separately:

- `prefer_toolkit_libdevice`: whether Inductor should opportunistically use CUDA toolkit libdevice when found.
- `require_toolkit_libdevice`: whether missing toolkit libdevice is notable enough to warn because the user requested eager-like numerics.

Suggested policy:

1. If `TRITON_LIBDEVICE_PATH` is set, use it. This remains the highest-priority explicit override.
2. If `triton.knobs.nvidia.libdevice_path` is already set, respect it.
3. Otherwise, try `CUDA_HOME/nvvm/libdevice/libdevice.10.bc`.
4. If that file exists:
   - set `knobs.nvidia.libdevice_path`;
   - set `os.environ["TRITON_LIBDEVICE_PATH"]` so async compile workers inherit the same choice.
5. If toolkit libdevice is not found:
   - if `require_toolkit_libdevice` is true, warn and fall back to Triton's bundled libdevice;
   - otherwise silently fall back to Triton's bundled libdevice.

`require_toolkit_libdevice` should remain:

```python
require_toolkit_libdevice = (
    config.eager_numerics.use_pytorch_libdevice or config.emulate_precision_casts
)
```

The default path should prefer but not require toolkit libdevice:

```python
prefer_toolkit_libdevice = True
```

## Implementation Sketch

Current entry point:

```python
def _set_triton_libdevice_path() -> None:
    from torch._inductor import config

    if not (
        config.eager_numerics.use_pytorch_libdevice or config.emulate_precision_casts
    ):
        return

    _set_triton_libdevice_path_impl()
```

Proposed shape:

```python
def _set_triton_libdevice_path() -> None:
    from torch._inductor import config

    require_toolkit_libdevice = (
        config.eager_numerics.use_pytorch_libdevice or config.emulate_precision_casts
    )

    _set_triton_libdevice_path_impl(
        prefer_toolkit_libdevice=True,
        require_toolkit_libdevice=require_toolkit_libdevice,
    )
```

Then update `_set_triton_libdevice_path_impl` to accept those booleans and only emit fallback warnings when `require_toolkit_libdevice` is true.

The async worker propagation logic can remain as-is. It already forwards `TRITON_LIBDEVICE_PATH` to subprocess compile workers and sets `knobs.nvidia.libdevice_path` in the worker.

## Compatibility and Risk

This changes the default libdevice source on machines with a full CUDA toolkit. That can affect:

- generated PTX;
- performance of transcendental-heavy kernels;
- small numerical differences in functions implemented by libdevice;
- cache keys and cache invalidation behavior.

The risk is acceptable if the selected external libdevice remains part of the Triton/Inductor cache key. The current PyTorch source already has extern-library cache validation hooks, so the implementation should verify that the resolved libdevice path and contents are represented there.

The proposal intentionally avoids making toolkit libdevice a hard requirement. Many PyTorch wheel users have CUDA runtime libraries but no full CUDA toolkit or `CUDA_HOME`. Those users should continue to compile successfully with Triton's bundled libdevice and should not see warnings during ordinary `torch.compile` use.


### Alternatives

_No response_

### Additional context

issues.author: eqy
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

#183521 appears to have introduced a regression in models such as Stable Diffusion due to changes in conv fusions. Minimal repro attached

bad
```
latency_ms=mean=122.874 p50=122.677 p90=123.610 min=122.045
```
good
```
latency_ms=mean=20.421 p50=20.430 p90=20.464 min=20.313
```

repro commands:

```
  TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/ti_repro_on \
  python minimal_inductor_repro.py \
    --variant residual_upsample_conv_skipconv \
    --channels 256 \
    --input-size 128 \
    --iters 6 \
    --warmup 2
```

```
  TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/ti_repro_off \
  TORCHINDUCTOR_LOOP_REINDEXING_AFTER_FUSION=0 \
  python minimal_inductor_repro.py \
    --variant residual_upsample_conv_skipconv \
    --channels 256 \
    --input-size 128 \
    --iters 6 \
    --warmup 2
```

```    
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import argparse
import os
import statistics
import time

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch._inductor import config, metrics


class UpsampleConvGroupNormSilu(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, channels: int, groups: int) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.conv = nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.norm = nn.GroupNorm(groups, channels, eps=1e-6)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        x = F.interpolate(x, scale_factor=2.0, mode="nearest")
        x = self.conv(x)
        x = self.norm(x)
        return F.silu(x)


class UpsampleConvGroupNormSiluResidual(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, channels: int, groups: int) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.conv = nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.norm = nn.GroupNorm(groups, channels, eps=1e-6)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        x = F.interpolate(x, scale_factor=2.0, mode="nearest")
        x = self.conv(x)
        y = F.silu(self.norm(x))
        return y + (x * 0.01)


class UpsampleConvGroupNormSiluSkipConv(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, channels: int, groups: int) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.conv = nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.norm = nn.GroupNorm(groups, channels, eps=1e-6)
        self.skip = nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, kernel_size=1)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        x = F.interpolate(x, scale_factor=2.0, mode="nearest")
        x = self.conv(x)
        y = F.silu(self.norm(x))
        skip = self.skip(x)
        return y + (skip * 0.01)


class ResidualUpsampleConvGroupNormSiluSkipConv(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, channels: int, groups: int) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.conv = nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.norm = nn.GroupNorm(groups, channels, eps=1e-6)
        self.skip = nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, kernel_size=1)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor, residual: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        x = (x + residual) / 1.41421356237
        x = F.interpolate(x, scale_factor=2.0, mode="nearest")
        x = self.conv(x)
        y = F.silu(self.norm(x))
        skip = self.skip(x)
        return y + (skip * 0.01)


class UpsampleGroupNormSilu(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, channels: int, groups: int) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.norm = nn.GroupNorm(groups, channels, eps=1e-6)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        x = F.interpolate(x, scale_factor=2.0, mode="nearest")
        x = self.norm(x)
        return F.silu(x)


class GroupNormSilu(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, channels: int, groups: int) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.norm = nn.GroupNorm(groups, channels, eps=1e-6)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        x = self.norm(x)
        return F.silu(x)


def percentile(values: list[float], pct: float) -> float:
    if not values:
        return float("nan")
    ordered = sorted(values)
    idx = round((len(ordered) - 1) * pct / 100.0)
    return ordered[idx]


def synchronize(device: torch.device) -> None:
    if device.type == "cuda":
        torch.cuda.synchronize(device)


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--batch", type=int, default=64)
    parser.add_argument("--channels", type=int, default=256)
    parser.add_argument("--groups", type=int, default=32)
    parser.add_argument("--input-size", type=int, default=8)
    parser.add_argument(
        "--variant",
        choices=(
            "upsample_conv",
            "upsample_conv_residual",
            "upsample_conv_skipconv",
            "residual_upsample_conv_skipconv",
            "upsample_norm",
            "norm",
        ),
        default="upsample_norm",
    )
    parser.add_argument("--channels-last", action="store_true")
    parser.add_argument("--warmup", type=int, default=5)
    parser.add_argument("--iters", type=int, default=30)
    parser.add_argument("--eager", action="store_true")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    if not torch.cuda.is_available():
        raise RuntimeError("CUDA is required for this reproducer")

    torch.manual_seed(0)
    torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = True
    torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 = True

    device = torch.device("cuda")
    if args.variant == "upsample_conv":
        model = UpsampleConvGroupNormSilu(args.channels, args.groups)
    elif args.variant == "upsample_conv_residual":
        model = UpsampleConvGroupNormSiluResidual(args.channels, args.groups)
    elif args.variant == "upsample_conv_skipconv":
        model = UpsampleConvGroupNormSiluSkipConv(args.channels, args.groups)
    elif args.variant == "residual_upsample_conv_skipconv":
        model = ResidualUpsampleConvGroupNormSiluSkipConv(args.channels, args.groups)
    elif args.variant == "upsample_norm":
        model = UpsampleGroupNormSilu(args.channels, args.groups)
    else:
        model = GroupNormSilu(args.channels, args.groups)

    model = model.eval().to(device)
    if args.channels_last:
        model = model.to(memory_format=torch.channels_last)

    x = torch.randn(
        args.batch,
        args.channels,
        args.input_size,
        args.input_size,
        device=device,
    )
    if args.channels_last:
        x = x.to(memory_format=torch.channels_last)
    residual = torch.randn_like(x) if args.variant.startswith("residual_") else None

    compiled = model if args.eager else torch.compile(model, mode="reduce-overhead")

    metrics.reset()
    with torch.no_grad():
        for _ in range(args.warmup):
            y = compiled(x, residual) if residual is not None else compiled(x)
        synchronize(device)
        generated_kernel_count = metrics.generated_kernel_count

        times_ms = []
        for _ in range(args.iters):
            start = time.perf_counter()
            y = compiled(x, residual) if residual is not None else compiled(x)
            synchronize(device)
            times_ms.append((time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000.0)

    # Keep the output live without adding work to the timed loop.
    checksum = float(y.mean().detach().cpu())

    print(f"torch={torch.__version__}")
    print(f"device={torch.cuda.get_device_name(device)}")
    print(
        "loop_reindexing_after_fusion="
        f"{os.environ.get('TORCHINDUCTOR_LOOP_REINDEXING_AFTER_FUSION', '<default>')}"
    )
    print(
        "inductor_config="
        f"loop_reindexing_after_fusion={config.loop_reindexing_after_fusion} "
        f"loop_ordering_after_fusion={config.loop_ordering_after_fusion}"
    )
    print(
        "shape="
        f"input=({args.batch}, {args.channels}, {args.input_size}, {args.input_size}) "
        f"output=({args.batch}, {args.channels}, "
        f"{args.input_size * (1 if args.variant == 'norm' else 2)}, "
        f"{args.input_size * (1 if args.variant == 'norm' else 2)}) "
        f"groups={args.groups} variant={args.variant} "
        f"channels_last={args.channels_last}"
    )
    print(f"generated_kernel_count={generated_kernel_count}")
    print(
        "latency_ms="
        f"mean={statistics.mean(times_ms):.3f} "
        f"p50={statistics.median(times_ms):.3f} "
        f"p90={percentile(times_ms, 90):.3f} "
        f"min={min(times_ms):.3f}"
    )
    print(f"checksum={checksum:.6f}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

issues.author: latentCall145

### 🐛 Describe the bug

When running a residual block, I noticed that compiled networks that have a 1x1 skip convolution use less memory when applied to all layers rather than just layers where the number of channels change. Up to a certain input size, the program OOMs only when 1x1 convs happen in the layers with changing channel counts. I would expect the opposite because applying 1x1 convs to all layers would add parameters thus increasing memory usage. 


Also, this is not the case if there is no normalization and activation happens after the convolution. Is this just a quirk of the compile function? I know that pre-activation is not the norm but it seems to have produced better results here: https://towardsdatascience.com/resnet-with-identity-mapping-over-1000-layers-reached-image-classification-bb50a42af03e

Code to reproduce:

```python
        x = x if self.skip is None else self.skip(x)
        return h + x

device = 'cuda'

            model = torch.compile(model)
            print('N params:', sum([p.numel() for p in model.parameters()]))
            x = torch.zeros((8, 256, 64, 64)).to(device)
```

issues.title: [Inductor][CuTeDSL] Repeated captured loads expand pre-lowering IR
issues.author: drisspg
issues.body:
### Problem

CuTeDSL modification lowering materializes captured-tensor index and value fragments before the existing expression CSE sees the final `.load()`. As a result, an exact repeated read such as `midpoint[kv_idx]` emits duplicate fragment setup in generated Python and expands the pre-lowering MLIR. The `cute-to-nvvm` pipeline eventually removes the duplicate, so the final PTX/SASS and runtime are unchanged, but compilation does unnecessary work.

On an exact production-shaped GB300 FlexAttention workload (BF16, Q `[1, 32768, 16, 64]`, K/V `[1, 98304, 2, 64]`, deterministic 2K block-sparse window), manually reusing the first captured load produced:

| Measurement | Before | With early CSE | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| First forward compile + call | 8,484.8 ms | 7,993.5 ms | -5.8% |
| First backward compile + call | 6,907.2 ms | 6,359.0 ms | -7.9% |
| Forward main MLIR pipeline | 3,223.8 ms | 2,975.3 ms | -7.7% |
| Backward main MLIR pipeline | 1,210.3 ms | 1,202.0 ms | -0.7% |

Pre-pipeline MLIR size decreased 2.2% forward and 9.2% backward. Post-pipeline MLIR, PTX, cubin, and disassembled SASS were byte-identical.

A narrow fix is to reuse exact repeated captured loads within one read-only modification handler, keyed by buffer name and symbolic index. Different buffers and different indices must remain distinct.

> **AI assistance disclosure:** An AI coding assistant helped inspect the lowering path, prepare the benchmark harness, and draft this issue. I reviewed the lowering behavior, generated code, and reported measurements.

### Analysis

This is a **performance regression on AArch64 CPU** that appeared after migrating the Inductor benchmark jobs to the OSDC (ARC) arm64 runners in #187994. The comparison table shows large jumps in **Abs Execution Time** while accuracy stays `pass` and **Portable speedup stays roughly constant**, e.g.:

| Model | Abs exec time (pre → post) | Approx factor |
|---|---|---|
| `mobilenetv2_100` | 52.68ms → 158.30ms | ~3.0x |
| `deit_base_distilled_patch16_224` | 308.31ms → 514.01ms | ~1.7x |
| `mobilenetv3_large_100` | 309.20ms → 481.61ms | ~1.6x |
| `repvgg_a2` | 190.96ms → 292.04ms | ~1.5x |
| `ghostnet_100` | 138.14ms → 152.06ms | ~1.1x |

**Key signal:** the *speedup* (compiled vs. eager) is essentially unchanged, and you note eager regressed by a similar amount. That points away from a `torch.compile`/Inductor codegen regression and toward the **runner environment itself** — i.e. the new ARC arm64 hosts are measuring slower wall-clock than the previous runners. Common causes for this pattern after a runner migration:

- Different/older Neoverse core generation or lower sustained clocks (no turbo / power policy)
- Fewer vCPUs or different thread/affinity defaults (`OMP_NUM_THREADS`, core pinning, NUMA)
- Noisy-neighbor / shared-host contention or thermal throttling on the new fleet
- Different glibc / kernel / BLAS (e.g. OpenBLAS vs. Arm Compute Library) or `LD_PRELOAD` / allocator differences baked into the new image

Since absolute timings are not normalized across heterogeneous hardware, a runner migration legitimately shifts the baseline. The actionable question for whoever owns the benchmark fleet is whether the new ARC arm64 runners are spec-equivalent (CPU model, core count, threading env) to the pre-migration ones, and whether a fresh baseline needs to be captured for the dashboard.

### Suggested next diagnostics
- Compare `lscpu` / `nproc` / governor and the `OMP_NUM_THREADS` + thread-affinity settings between the old and new runner images.
- Confirm the same BLAS/ACL backend and version are present in both images.
- If the new fleet is intentionally different hardware, the benchmark dashboard baseline likely needs to be re-seeded post-migration rather than treated as a code regression.

Based on the [triage rubric](.claude/skills/triaging-issues), this is a CI-infrastructure-driven performance regression on ARM (root cause is the runner migration, not PT2 codegen), so:

- `module: arm`

comments.body:
Root-caused and validated. The aarch64 perf runner was not on the hardware its label implied.

## Cause

`linux.arm64.m8g.metal-24xl` maps to the OSDC runner `l-barm64g4-94-344`, which was defined on a virtualized `m8g.24xlarge` as a stand-in for the real `m8g.metal-24xl`. Worse, its fleet (`m8g-large`) lists `m8g.48xlarge` at weight 100, so Karpenter was actually provisioning a **192-core / 768 GiB** node and running the 94-core job on part of it.

Graviton4 is 96 cores per socket, so `m8g.48xlarge` is two sockets / two NUMA nodes. The 94-core cgroup straddled both and paid cross-socket memory traffic on every iteration — which is exactly the kind of thing that inflates absolute wall clock while leaving the inductor-vs-eager ratio intact.

The benchmark records themselves confirm the backing. `runners[0]` from the uploaded results:

```
nightlies on main   cpu_count=192  avail_mem_in_gb=742    <- m8g.48xlarge, dual-socket
mock run on metal   cpu_count=96   avail_mem_in_gb=376    <- m8g.metal-24xl, single socket
```

## Fix and validation

pytorch/ci-infra#969 re-points the runner to a real `m8g.metal-24xl` on a dedicated single-instance fleet, so no virtualized node can be substituted in. Validated with #191823, which routes this workflow at the staging cluster where that change is deployed.

Mock run vs the median of three `main` nightlies (`inference` / `bfloat16`, config parity verified: `repeat=30, iterations=2, batch_size=None, threads=None`):

| Metric | Median delta | Improved |
|---|---|---|
| `abs_latency` | **-49.7%** | 291 / 292 models |
| `compilation_latency` | -4.0% | 230 / 286 |
| `speedup` (relative) | -3.5% | flat |

By suite, `abs_latency`: huggingface -41.6% (n=103), torchbench -73.4% (n=189).

Examples (ms, `inductor_aot_inductor`):

```
BartForCausalLM                  497.5 -> 263.4   -47%
ElectraForCausalLM               263.3 -> 133.8   -49%
M2M100ForConditionalGeneration   710.8 -> 352.2   -50%
BertForMaskedLM                  491.5 -> 273.8   -44%
AlbertForMaskedLM               1675.8 -> 1280.4  -24%
```

This reproduces the decoupling reported here, in reverse: absolute time halves while relative speedup stays flat. It also ran on *fewer* cores (92 vs 94), so this is not "more CPU".

Data: `s3://ossci-benchmarks/v3/pytorch/pytorch/{workflow_id}/`, workflow `30680927631` (metal) vs `30738497917` / `30690425905` / `30614840265` (baseline).

comments.body: it's an ordering bug, not flaky. `test_custom_op_symm_mem_realization` passes on its own but fails when the file or the whole LoweringTest class runs because Inductor generates the persistent symm-mem `alloc_id` with `random.randint(0, 2**64-1)` at codegen time and our test harness reseeds `random.seed(1234)` in `TestCase.setUp` before every test (common_utils.py), so the first randint draw is always the same value i.e., `14354624986284130233`, which isexactly the `alloc_id` in the traceback.. It's worth noting this isn't purely a test artifact since `alloc_id` comes from the globally-seeded random, any user code that calls `random.seed()` before `torch.compile()` on symm-mem collectives can hit the same collision. We should source `alloc_id` from `secrets.randbits(64)` instead of the global random as it only needs to be process-unique and is baked into the generated code as a constant, so entropy-based generation is both sufficient and immune to reseeding. Full `test_symmetric_memory.py` passes with it. PR coming shortly.

issues.title: BUG: Inductor `as_strided` silently reads out of bounds
issues.author: KyleMylonakisProtopia
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

When a tensor that is a view with a non-zero `storage_offset` is passed as a mutated pointer argument to a raw `triton.jit` kernel, `torch.compile` silently produces an incorrect result. This is due to data being read from beyond the end of a buffer into memory.

The over-read is normally invisible because the kernel overwrites the whole region. The edge case is when the kernel skips writing part of its output as a performance optimization. E.G "if this row is masked/ignored, return early".

This bug was originally found when compiling Liger-Kernel's `LigerFusedLinearJSD`  and `LigerFusedLinearCrossEntropy` functions, where it silently corrupted outputs returning incorrect losses compared to eager execution whenever any label was `ignore_index` was present. Both of these failures can be silent.
I introduced a workaround with Liger at https://github.com/linkedin/Liger-Kernel/pull/1338, however the bug is fundamentally in PyTorch.

## Reproduction

With AI assistance, I created a script which depends only on `torch` and `triton`. The script poisons the caching allocator so the
corruption is identifiable. The usual `compute-sanitizer --tool memcheck` does not flag this, because CUDA mappings are page-granular and a small over-read still lands in mapped memory. In other words, when the overruns are small enough, you land in your paged memory pool, which is still technically owned by the process and doesn't immediately fault.

The reproduction script is

```python
import torch, triton, triton.language as tl

N, R, SKIP, POISON, DEV = 2048, 4, 1, 12345.0, "cuda"

@triton.jit
def maybe_fill(out_ptr, do_write, n_cols, BLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    """Fill out_ptr[0:n_cols] with 1.0, but only when do_write != 0."""
    if do_write != 0:
        offs = tl.arange(0, BLOCK)
        tl.store(out_ptr + offs, 1.0, mask=offs < n_cols)

def run():
    base = torch.zeros(R, N, device=DEV, dtype=torch.float32)
    for i in range(R):
        row = base[i : i + 1]                       # view, storage_offset = i * N
        maybe_fill[(1,)](row, 0 if i == SKIP else 1, N, BLOCK=N)
        base[i : i + 1] = row                       # write-back
    return base

def poison_allocator(count=2048):
    junk = [torch.full((N,), POISON, device=DEV, dtype=torch.float32) for _ in range(count)]
    del junk
    torch.cuda.synchronize()

expected = torch.zeros(R, N, device=DEV)
expected[[i for i in range(R) if i != SKIP]] = 1.0

poison_allocator(); eager = run().clone()
cf = torch.compile(run, fullgraph=True); cf()      # compile before poisoning
poison_allocator(); compiled = cf().clone()

print("eager    matches:", torch.equal(eager, expected))
print("compiled matches:", torch.equal(compiled, expected))
print("freed-memory value present:", int((compiled == POISON).sum()), "elements")
```

Row `SKIP` is never written by the kernel, so it must remain zero in both runs.

**Observed:**

```text
eager    matches: True
compiled matches: False
freed-memory value present: 2048 elements
```

The poison value `12345.0` never exists in live tensors. It is written into memory that was freed before the call. Its presence is direct evidence of an out-of-bounds read.

### Mechanism

Three different pieces interact to cause the bug. The first two are individually reasonable. The third breaks an
assumption the second one depends on.

1. Functionalizing a mutated Triton pointer arg clones it via
   `torch._prims_common.clone_preserve_strides`.

2. To preserve the view's layout, that helper has to clone `storage_offset + span` elements out of the tensor's storage, not just the tensor's own elements:

   ```python
   needed_size = compute_required_storage_length(x.size(), x.stride(), x.storage_offset())
   buffer = torch.as_strided(x, (needed_size,), (1,), 0).clone()
   return torch.as_strided(buffer, x.size(), x.stride(), x.storage_offset())
   ```

   For `base[1:2]` of a `(4, 2048)` tensor that is `2048 + 2048 = 4096` elements. This is correct in eager, where the base storage genuinely has 8192 elements to read from.

3. Inductor's `as_strided` lowering has two paths. Which one it takes depends on whether the incoming tensor is still a view:

   - `x` is an unrealized view over a larger buffer, the lowering unwraps to that buffer, so the offset is resolved against storage that really exists. This is the case the code was written for, and it is fine.
   - `x` has already been materialized into its own buffer: the lowering takes that buffer as the storage. Inductor materializes a view when it is the output of a fused computation, which is exactly what the `slice_scatter` chain from the write-back produces.

   In the second case the storage is the small buffer of say 2048 elements, and the lowering builds a `ReinterpretView` describing 4096 elements. Nothing checks that the requested `ReinterpretView` extent fits.

So the invariant that breaks is this: `aten.as_strided`'s `storage_offset` is relative to the
whole storage, but Inductor resolves it against whichever buffer happened to get realized. Those are the same thing right up until a view gets materialized into a buffer sized to the view, and then the lowering is describing memory that was never allocated.

From `TORCH_LOGS=output_code`:

```python
buf3 = empty_strided_cuda((1, 2048), (2048, 1), torch.float32)   # 2048 elements
buf4 = empty_strided_cuda((4096, ), (1, ), torch.float32)
triton_poi_fused_2.run(buf3, buf4, 4096)      # <-- reads 4096 elements out of buf3
maybe_fill_1.run(reinterpret_tensor(buf4, (1, 2048), (2048, 1), 2048), 0, ...)
```

The offending Inductor generated kernel. Note how the read is unmasked:

```python
def triton_poi_fused_2(in_ptr0, out_ptr0, xnumel, XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    xnumel = 4096
    xmask = tl.full([XBLOCK], True, tl.int1)[:]   # unmasked
    x0 = xindex
    tmp0 = tl.load(in_ptr0 + (x0), None)          # 2048 elements past the end of buf3
    tl.store(out_ptr0 + (x0), tmp0, None)
```

`maybe_fill_1` then receives `buf4 + 2048`, which is precisely the garbage half. Because `do_write == 0` it never writes there, so the garbage survives into the output.

It gets worse further into the loop, since the buffer sizes track `needed_size`: 4096 / 6144 / 8192 for rows 1 / 2 / 3. Each of those still reads out of a 2048-element source, so the last iteration over-reads by 6144 elements.

This is a PyTorch bug, not a Triton one. The out-of-bounds load is in an Inductor-generated kernel: `tl.load(in_ptr0 + x0, None)` with `xnumel = 4096` carries no bounds information and Triton has no way to know `in_ptr0` is only 2048 elements long. The mutation analysis that decides which args are mutated is correct here.

### What hides this bug

- `do_write` must be a runtime arg, not `tl.constexpr`. As a constexpr, Triton compiles the store away, the pointer is no longer seen as mutated, so no clone is emitted.
- The mutated arg must be a view whose required extent exceeds its own numel. A non-zero `storage_offset` or gaps between elements must be present.
- Some runtime path must skip writing, or the garbage is always overwritten.
- The bug is is shape-dependent. It reproduces at `N = 2048` but not at `N = 1 << 20` because Inductor makes different realization choices.
- The view must be realized as its own buffer. A single kernel launch on `base[1:2]` with no surrounding computation does not reproduce the bug. The loop with write-backs creates the `slice_scatter` chain that forces per-view realization.

### Versions

Reproduced on `2.14.0a0+git0a2b9b3` with triton 3.8.0, and on `2.13.0+cu130` / `2.12.1+cu130`
with triton 3.7.1. NVIDIA GB10, `sm_121`, Ubuntu 24.04 aarch64, Python 3.12 / 3.10.

Also reproduces with `fullgraph=False`, with `dynamic=True`, and under `inference_mode` and
`no_grad`.

issues.author: guilhermeleobas
issues.body:
`bytearray` has no `VariableTracker` model in Dynamo and any attempt to use it will result in a graph break. We want to close this gap as `bytearray` seems to be used by some libraries under the hood. 

## Current state

Probed on `main` with `torch.compile(fn, backend="eager", fullgraph=True)`.
Each row is roughly `torch.compile(lambda b: <op>, backend="eager",
fullgraph=True)(bytearray(b"abc"))`.

| operation | result |
| --- | --- |
| `bytearray()` / `bytearray(3)` / `bytearray([1,2,3])` / `bytearray(b"abc")` / `bytearray("abc", "utf-8")` | `Unsupported: Failed to trace builtin operator` |
| pass a `bytearray` arg straight through | works |
| `b == b"abc"` | works |
| `isinstance(b, bytearray)` | works |
| `len(b)` | `Unsupported: C-implemented special method without VariableTracker model` |
| `b[1]`, `b[1:]`, `b[0] = 65` | same as above |
| `iter(b)` / `list(b)`, `98 in b` | same as above |
| `b.append(65)`, `b.extend(b"cd")`, `b += b"cd"` | `Unsupported: Failed to trace builtin operator` |
| `bytes(b)`, `memoryview(b)` | `Unsupported: Failed to trace builtin operator` |
| `b.decode()`, `b.hex()` | `Unsupported: Unsupported method call` |
| `b * 2` | `Unsupported: sq_repeat_impl not implemented` |
| mutating a `bytearray` passed in as an arg | `Unsupported: Unsupported method call` |
| `torch.frombuffer(b, dtype=torch.uint8)` | `Unsupported: Failed to convert args/kwargs to proxy` |
| `bytearray` subclass instantiation | `Unsupported: Unsupported function call` |

Three of the 26 probed operations work today.

## Scope of work
1. Port the CPython test suite
CPython has no `test_bytearray.py`; `bytearray` coverage lives in
`Lib/test/test_bytes.py` (~2657 lines), shared with `bytes` via a common base
class.

2. Add a `ByteArrayVariable(VariableTracker)` with support for sequence / mapping / number protocols, methods (using `tp_methods`), iteration, etc. Not everything needs to be done in the same PR and follow-ups are ok.

3. Fix the corner cases the port surfaces
